opus-5.5.text:
I think the simplest way to understand it is through token efficiency. High-quality data is fundamentally limited. The amount of good human-written text on the internet is finite, and we're already consuming a large fraction of it. So the question becomes: given the same tokens, how much intelligence can you extract from them?

A better optimizer effectively changes the exchange rate between data and capability. If your optimizer is more efficient, the same dataset behaves as if it were larger. You reach the same loss with fewer tokens, or a lower loss with the same tokens. In a world where data is the bottleneck rather than compute, that matters enormously.

Part of why we spent effort on things like Muon is that Adam has been the default for so long that people treat it almost as a law of nature. It isn't. Adam treats each parameter fairly independently. But the weights in a neural network are matrices, and they have structure. If your update respects that structure, for example by orthogonalizing the update so you don't keep pushing in a few dominant directions, each step can make more useful progress. Every gradient step carries more information from the data.

There's also a deeper point. Lower loss is not just a number on a chart. Pretraining loss correlates quite strongly with downstream ability: reasoning, knowledge, generalization. So if a better optimizer gives you a meaningfully lower loss at the same data budget, that translates into a smarter base model. Everything you do afterward, like RL or agentic training, builds on that foundation.

Of course, it isn't free. When you scale a new optimizer to very large models, you run into stability problems. Logits can blow up and training can diverge. A lot of the real work is engineering the details so the efficiency gain survives at scale instead of only looking good on small experiments. But once you get it working, I think it's one of the most leveraged improvements you can make. You're not adding more data or compute. You're just learning more from what you already have.

r001.rationale: The response says a better optimizer extracts more capability from the same tokens, making the same dataset behave as if it were larger and enabling lower loss with the same token budget.

fable-5.1.text:
The simplest way I think about it is: a better optimizer gives you more intelligence per token. If you hold the data fixed, the optimizer determines how much of the signal in that data actually gets absorbed into the weights. With something like AdamW, a lot of that signal is wasted, either because the steps are poorly conditioned or because you have to use a smaller learning rate to stay stable. With a better optimizer, like Muon, every step extracts more from the same batch, so the loss curve drops faster and reaches a lower point for the same number of tokens.

Why this matters so much right now is that data has become the real bottleneck. For a long time, the scaling story was that you just add more compute and more data together. But high-quality tokens on the internet are finite, and we are already close to running through them. Once data is the constraint, the question is no longer "how do I get more tokens," it is "how do I get more out of each token." Optimizer improvements are one of the few levers that directly address that.

Our experience has been that when you measure it carefully, a good optimizer behaves like a roughly constant multiplier on token efficiency. In the Moonlight experiments, Muon reached the same loss as AdamW with somewhere around half the training compute, and that advantage held as we scaled up. It wasn't a trick that disappeared at larger sizes. That is important, because many ideas look good at small scale and then vanish.

There is also a second-order effect that people underestimate. Because the optimizer is more stable, you can push the learning rate harder and train longer without the model blowing up. For a very large model like Kimi K2, with a trillion parameters trained on fifteen trillion tokens, we had essentially no loss spikes. That stability is itself a form of efficiency, since you don't waste runs or have to roll back.

So the way I'd summarize it is: with the same data, a better optimizer is equivalent to having more data. And in a world where data is the scarce resource, that equivalence is worth a lot.

r001.rationale: The response says a better optimizer extracts more signal from each batch and makes the model learn more from the same data.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to distinguish the amount of data from how effectively the model learns from it. Even if two models see exactly the same training tokens, different optimizers can produce different results. A better optimizer can use the gradients more effectively, so within the same training budget, the model gets closer to a good solution.

You can think of that as an improvement in learning efficiency: either you reach the same performance with fewer training steps, or you get better performance from the same amount of data. Of course, lower training loss doesn’t automatically mean better generalization, so ultimately you need to check whether the improvement carries over to held-out data and the tasks you care about.

r001.rationale: It says that with the same training tokens, a better optimizer can use gradients more effectively and improve learning efficiency.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to distinguish how much data the model sees from how much it learns from that data. Even with exactly the same training examples, different optimizers can lead to different results. A better optimizer can make each update more effective, so the model reaches a lower loss within the same training budget.

You can think of it as improving learning efficiency. One way to improve a model is to give it more data; another is to help it extract more from the data it already has. Of course, lower training loss doesn’t automatically mean better performance on new tasks, so ultimately you need to check whether that optimization improvement translates into better generalization.

r001.rationale: It says a better optimizer can make each update more effective and help the model extract more from the same training examples.
